golden_qa.question: What changed in version 0.18.1?
golden_qa.answer: 0.18.1 is a packaging fix with no rule changes. numpy, soundfile and ttsproof were hard runtime dependencies used by exactly one module, the speech dataset checker, and the CLI imported it at module scope. So installing trainproof pulled an audio stack, and linting a text log would not start without libsndfile, the C library behind soundfile. The core now declares no runtime dependencies at all; those three moved to an optional trainproof[speech] extra, and the speech import is lazy. 274 tests pass and all 18 fault-injection verdicts are byte-identical to 0.18.0.

golden_qa.question: Does trainproof have any dependencies?
golden_qa.answer: No. As of 0.18.1 the core declares no runtime dependencies. Reading a TensorBoard event file needs no tensorflow, tensorboard, protobuf or torch, because the tfevents reader is written from the wire format and validated byte-exact against EventAccumulator. The speech and TTS dataset checker needs numpy, soundfile and ttsproof, and those install only if you ask for trainproof[speech].

golden_qa.question: Why does a linter for training logs care about audio libraries?
golden_qa.answer: It should not, and as of 0.18.1 it does not. trainproof has a speech and TTS dataset pack that genuinely needs soundfile to read audio. The mistake was that the CLI imported that pack eagerly, so everyone paid for it. It is now an optional extra and the import happens only when a speech command is actually called.

golden_qa.question: How many rules does trainproof have?
golden_qa.answer: 90 distinct TP-* rule IDs at 0.18.1, unchanged from 0.18.0 since that release added no rules. A test enforces that the IDs in the source and the IDs documented in RULES.md match in both directions, so an undocumented rule and an orphaned doc entry both fail the build.

golden_qa.question: What is trainproof for?
golden_qa.answer: It reads the training logs you already produce and returns a verdict with an exit code, so you can stop paying for a run that is already dead. No model judges a model and there are no confidence scores: every check is a deterministic rule that either fires or does not, and prints the number it fired on. It reads Hugging Face trainer_state.json, Coqui logs, TensorBoard event files, JSONL and CSV.

golden_qa.question: What does trainproof do when it cannot judge a run?
golden_qa.answer: It says so. NOT-CHECKED is a distinct verdict with its own exit code, 2, separate from FAIL at 1 and PASS at 0. A tool that cannot tell "your run failed" from "I could not read your log" is lying to your CI quietly. Every single-run report also carries a checks object listing which check groups ran and why each of the rest did not.

golden_qa.question: What can trainproof not catch?
golden_qa.answer: A model learning the wrong thing, from a single run's curve. In the fault-injection study, a run trained on shuffled labels dropped its loss from 18.9 to 5.7 and looked textbook-healthy while memorising the statistics of noise. That is indistinguishable from real training on one curve. Catching it needs trainproof compare against a known-good baseline, where it fails on all three seeds. The limitation is stated in the README rather than left for a user to discover.

golden_qa.question: How were trainproof's rules validated?
golden_qa.answer: Against a controlled fault-injection study: one Qwen2.5-3B QLoRA in six configurations, healthy, 100x learning rate, lr=0, fp16 NaN, shuffled labels and overfit, three seeds each, eighteen runs. The 100x learning-rate run spiked its gradient norm to about 2,650, roughly 4,900 times its own median. The results table is generated from the logs by a script, and a test fails the build if the published table drifts from the data it describes.

golden_qa.question: Has a real training log ever proved trainproof wrong?
golden_qa.answer: Yes, and the fix is documented. TP-ZERO-GRAD fired whenever every gradient norm was exactly 0.0 and reported a severed backward graph. Coqui writes avg_grad_norm as 0.0 when clipping is off, so a healthy 125,000-step run whose loss reached 0.017 got a FAIL from the tool itself. The fix was reasoning rather than a threshold: a run cannot both learn and receive no gradient, so the check stands down when the loss improved, and records why it stood down, because a check that did not run must never look like one that passed. No unit test caught that; one real log did.

golden_qa.question: Is trainproof related to ttsproof or spkproof?
golden_qa.answer: They are siblings, all MIT and all deterministic: trainproof judges training runs, ttsproof judges text-to-speech output, spkproof measures speaker verification. As of 0.18.1 trainproof's optional speech pack reuses ttsproof's text normalisation, which is why ttsproof appears in the trainproof[speech] extra rather than in the core.
